Integrative Review Outlines Multilevel Framework for Artificial Intelligence Justice in Public Health

A conceptual integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published in Frontiers in Public Health indicates that justice in public health artificial intelligence requires a dual focus on epistemic participation and material distribution across multiple systemic levels. Conducted by researcher Zhaohui Su of Southeast University, the synthesis evaluates how ethical concerns surrounding artificial intelligence are framed within health contexts, concluding that existing scholarship remains heavily concentrated on technical fairness, clinical accuracy, and individual-level decision-making while largely neglecting broader cross-scalar determinants. To resolve this conceptual fragmentation, the author proposes an adapted socio-ecological framework that organizes artificial intelligence justice into two foundational analytical dimensions: contributory justice, which examines whose knowledge, lived experiences, and values shape systems, and distributive justice, which analyzes how computational benefits, risks, operational burdens, and systemic harms are allocated across society. Rather than viewing machine learning tools solely as self-contained statistical algorithms, the framework conceptualizes public health technologies as components of interconnected socio-ecological environments spanning individual, social, organizational, geopolitical, and ecological scales.

The methodological architecture of the review relied on the established integrative review procedures formulated by Whittemore and Knafl, supplemented by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses screening framework. A targeted literature search conducted in April 2026 across the PubMed database utilized first-level Boolean search terms that combined artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and large language models with public health, global health, and healthcare, alongside justice and injustice terminology. From an initial pool of 582 identified records, 572 English-language publications underwent title and abstract screening. Following rigorous full-text evaluation against inclusion criteria requiring peer-reviewed status and an explicit analytical focus on artificial intelligence justice within public health, exactly 21 articles were selected for final qualitative synthesis. The included publications spanned from 2021 through 2026, reflecting a sharp emergence of critical investigations into epistemic harms, environmental consequences, community participation, and algorithmic resource allocation across diverse global medical and epidemiological applications.

The analytical core of the synthesized evidence distinguishes contributory justice from distributive justice as complementary, interacting lenses rather than mutually exclusive or empirically validated categories. Contributory justice investigates the degree to which patients, community members, and marginalized populations possess epistemic agency in designing, deploying, evaluating, and governing algorithmic systems. In contrast, distributive justice focuses on the material allocation of essential goods, technological opportunities, diagnostic accuracy, and adverse consequences across demographic groups. The review highlights that distributive injustice occurs when vulnerable populations face unequal access to advanced therapeutic interventions, disproportionate diagnostic errors, or unaddressed digital exclusion, whereas contributory injustice occurs when their descriptive accounts, localized perspectives, and unique health realities are systematically dismissed or distorted by dominant technical architectures. The synthesis underscores that unequal health outcomes alone do not automatically establish injustice without explicit normative criteria, emphasizing the necessity of clarifying whether equity evaluations prioritize meeting universal needs, securing fair equality of opportunity, or uplifting worst-off groups.

To structure these interrelated dimensions, the review adapts Urie Bronfenbrenner’s classic socio-ecological model into five operational levels representing nested tiers of influence: individual, social, organizational, geopolitical, and environmental domains. At the individual level, contributory concerns address how patient narratives and marginalized perspectives are routinely filtered, misclassified, or excluded from algorithmic training datasets and clinical trial designs, while distributive issues manifest as unequal diagnostic quality, biased risk scores, and accessibility barriers for linguistically or cognitively diverse groups. At the social level, the synthesis examines patient-provider interactions, showing that artificial intelligence intermediaries can undermine human credibility, shift epistemic authority toward automated systems, and exacerbate therapeutic imbalances. At the organizational level, spanning healthcare facilities, academic centers, and technology corporations, commercial priorities and computational metrics frequently overshadow participatory engagement, leading to uneven institutional deployment and disparate regional access to algorithmic governance guardrails and fairness auditing tools.

Beyond immediate institutional settings, the framework extends to geopolitical and environmental levels that have traditionally received peripheral attention in medical ethics. Geopolitically, the literature reveals stark global asymmetries wherein Western and high-income institutions dominate technical standards, while data extraction from low-resource regions occurs without proportional agency, consent, or equitable distribution of therapeutic innovations. Environmentally, the review connects massive computational infrastructures to broader ecological costs, noting how computational energy demands, pollution exposure, and regional infrastructure gaps disproportionately burden disadvantaged communities. The author contextualizes this ecological friction by examining regional energy disparities in China, where advanced solar development coexists with severe heatwave vulnerabilities, such as campus cooling shortages and fatal heatstrokes. While regional analyses demonstrate that industrial artificial intelligence adoption concentrates efficiency benefits within technologically advanced eastern provinces, the review explicitly notes that such macro-level energy discrepancies do not by themselves prove that public health algorithms directly caused particular population-level harms.

A chronological examination of the 21 included studies illustrates how scholarly conceptualizations of artificial intelligence justice have evolved over the past half-decade. Early foundational work identified in the corpus, such as a 2021 systematic scoping review on mental healthcare, introduced design justice principles centered on user empowerment, lived experience, and non-exploitative engagement. By 2023, scholarship increasingly integrated philosophical theories of epistemic injustice, analyzing how predictive models generate testimonial deficits by devaluing patient testimonies and producing hermeneutical gaps when algorithmic classifications override nuanced human communication. Studies examining automated opioid risk scores demonstrated how predictive scoring without adequate clinical oversight impairs diagnostic dialogue. Concurrently, theoretical contributions explored restorative paradigms, such as employing African Ubuntu philosophy—with its relational tenets of communalism, interdependence, humanism, sharing, and compassion—to counterbalance individualistic biases, mitigate power imbalances, and decolonize knowledge production across public health artificial intelligence systems.
